  • It has been revealed that tristen Epps-Long, Season 22 winner of Bravo's "Top Chef" and a former McDonald's chef, shared this savory-sweet Mickey D's menu hack in an exclusive interview with Food Republic.
  • Sources indicate that executing this McMuffin double-down is easy to do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that mcDonald's Egg McMuffin is an iconic sandwich within the fast food breakfast realm. The chain took the McMuffin from good to great when its restaurants began toasting the English muffin halves in real butter rather than margarine. Customers have also found their own methods for upgrading this legendary breakfast sandwich, such as adding hash brown patties into the mix or giving it a flavor twist with sweet add-ons. The latter practice actually harks back to the 1970s, when the sandwich was served with sugary condiments like honey and jam. While that didn't last long as a standard practice, you can still DIY your own sweet toppings to get twice the eating pleasure out of just one Egg McMuffin.

It has been revealed that tristen Epps-Long, Season 22 winner of Bravo's "Top Chef" and a former McDonald's chef, shared this savory-sweet Mickey D's menu hack in an exclusive interview with Food Republic. "I like to take my sandwich apart a little bit, so half of it becomes jellied and buttered and the other half of it becomes open-faced and savory," the expert shared.

Sources indicate that executing this McMuffin double-down is easy to do. Simply remove the sandwich's top English muffin half, exposing the Canadian bacon, egg, and cheese below. This provides the open-faced, savory portion to enjoy — nothing more to do. On the other muffin slice, apply your choice of the Strawberry Preserves or Grape Jam commonly offered at McD's restaurants (or you can combine the two to give your spread a mixed berry vibe). Voila! You have something satisfyingly sweet to crown your McMuffin feasting.

According to recent reports, when sweet meets salty, the resulting flavor wizardry is deeply satisfying. There are various other ways to apply this savory-sweet magic and take your McDonald's Egg McMuffin to the next level. Maple-flavored bacon is a popular breakfast staple, and you can bring that vibe to your McMuffin by pouring McDonald's Hotcake Syrup over the sandwich's Canadian bacon and letting it drip over the other elements. The maple-flavored sweetness brings a delightful dimension to the classic sandwich that is lip-smackingly scrumptious and the perfect foil for its salty heartiness.

It has been revealed that adding a packet of Mickey D's honey is another sweetening twist that gives your McMuffin honey ham flair. The honey is actually offered as a dipping sauce option for Chicken McNuggets, but no diehard Golden Arches diner will let that stop them from drizzling it onto a McMuffin for added sweetness.

In a recent development, mcDonald's also frequently releases promotional, limited-time sauces, many of which hit those sweet-savory notes with aplomb. Options like Hot Honey Sauce and spicy-sweet Hunter Sauce were among limited-time options that dropped in 2026. You don't have to strictly wait for a limited-edition sauce, though — Mickey D's Sweet 'N Sour Sauce and Creamy Chili McCrispy Strip Dip are on offer year-round to lend sweetness and other flavor dimensions to your Egg McMuffin.

Does Fluoride In Drinking Water Affect Intelligence? What The Evidence Reveals

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (398 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition?
  • Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition?
  • Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.

Researchers followed a generation of Wisconsin school-leavers, examining cognitive performance from adolescence into their eighties.

Those exposed to fluoridated water did not show a consistent disadvantage compared with people whose communities had no fluoridation.

The findings address concerns that adding fluoride to drinking water to prevent tooth decay could undermine intellectual development.

Professor John Robert Warren, the study’s first author, stated:.

“Utah, Florida and many municipalities have chosen to remove fluoride from drinking water based on flawed studies that considered the IQ effects of exposure to massive doses of fluoride.

Because levels of fluoride added to municipal drinking water in the U.S. are so much lower, almost all prior evidence from those international studies is not relevant to U.S. public policy debates.”.

The research draws on the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, which began with over 10,000 people who graduated from high school in 1957.

Researchers combined school IQ records with historical information about community water fluoridation and naturally occurring fluoride levels.

Following participants into old age allowed researchers to examine whether childhood exposure was associated with lasting differences in cognitive performance.

Comparing communities requires care because their residents can differ in ways that also relate to cognitive performance.

Once those background differences were taken into account, there was no consistent evidence that exposure was associated with either better or worse performance.

The same broad pattern appeared when researchers focused on people who had lived in the same county since early childhood, increasing confidence in their estimates of exposure.

Overall, the findings suggest that growing up with fluoridated community water is not associated with poorer cognitive performance in old age.

The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (Warren et al., 2026).

Not Butter, Oil, Or Lard: Chicken Skin Is 10x Crispier With This Rich Ingredient

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (399 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, top-notch crispy chicken skin can steal the show.
  • This under-utilized fat source is uber-savory, all while boasting a moderate smoke point.
  • Industry observers note that it's a technique compatible with many poultry cuts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, top-notch crispy chicken skin can steal the show. Sure, flavorful and juicy meat is tasty, but encased in a mouth-watering crispiness, the poultry experience only gets better. Achieving such a crackly bite entails light seasoning, low moisture, and – especially crucially – a good dose of rendered fat. Cooks often use butter, oil, or lard to improve crisping, but for an extra-rich rendition, reach for duck fat.

This under-utilized fat source is uber-savory, all while boasting a moderate smoke point. The ingredient comes as a firm paste at room temperature, meaning you'll need to melt the fat, then spread it onto the exterior of the chicken skin. The fat offers a two-for-one punch, adding both flavor and effectively crisping the skin as your chicken roasts.

Industry observers note that it's a technique compatible with many poultry cuts. In addition to an entire bird, you can add a touch to skin-on thighs or breasts, enhancing the dish in more subtle ways. Or dive in all the way and even fry your chicken in duck fat. In addition to chicken, you could make duck confit, cooking the protein in its own fat. Duck fat gives skin-on poultry that extra oomph, crisping up the skin to a delicious effect.

Not sure what to pair with duck fat-covered chicken? The add-in meshes with various flavors. Season and bake a whole bird with salt and pepper alongside the fat, and you've already got a mouth-watering rendition as-is. The duck fat also pairs well with herbal seasonings like dried thyme and oregano, as well as a generous dose of garlic.

You could also consider then roasting the chicken on a bed of vegetables, letting the rich fat drip down and flavor alliums and root vegetables. Or cook the bird in the same vessel as potatoes, which can be tossed in more duck fat for good measure. Roast potatoes are 10 times richer with this magical fat; in combination with the crispy chicken skin, you'll get a truly decadent meal.

In a recent development, the abundant richness could use some bright elements to cut through the fat. Squeeze on some lemon — both during and after the cooking process — or finish with a drizzle of balsamic. A sprinkling of parsley goes a long way, as does a crisp glass of wine, making chicken skin a special occasion.

#137994. Give Leftover Mashed Potatoes A Caramelized, Crispy Side With A British-Style Classic

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (580 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

Give Leftover Mashed Potatoes A Caramelized, Crispy Side With A British-Style Classic

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (580 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that not many dishes can compete with mashed potatoes.
  • According to recent reports, mashed potatoes fried in butter are part of an English comfort-food classic called bubble and squeak.
  • The potatoes need time to develop that crust.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that not many dishes can compete with mashed potatoes. Beyond being the ultimate comfort food, and dare we say, the best preparation of potatoes, it's also super budget-friendly, and any leftovers can be saved and used up later. But let's face it: Nothing beats freshly cooked mashed tots. You could pop leftovers in the microwave or oven to reheat them, but they often come out dry and lackluster. To give them a new lease of life, borrow a tip from the Brits (who know a thing or two about mash) and fry them in butter instead.

According to recent reports, mashed potatoes fried in butter are part of an English comfort-food classic called bubble and squeak. The dish is traditionally made from Sunday roast leftovers, with mash and cooked cabbage or other veg shallow-fried in butter, lard, or meat drippings until a crispy brown crust forms. That crust is what brings the leftovers back to life, so it's essential to let it form. This comes down to the Maillard reaction, which occurs when amino acids in the potatoes react with reducing sugars. For that to happen, you only need two things: heat and time.

The potatoes need time to develop that crust. If you drop them into the pan and start stirring them around, they'll warm through, but they won't form a base layer. Instead, pat the mash into an even layer in the pan and cook it undisturbed over medium heat for around five minutes, or until the underside is deeply golden. Then flip it and repeat. You'll hear it sizzle and pop as it fries, which is noted to be where the name bubble and squeak originates from.

In restaurants across the country, chefs are swapping high-end dining rooms for cozy neighborhood taverns – not to be confused with bars – serving food that's comforting, hearty, and nostalgic. Much of it looks like standard British pub grub, which makes bubble and squeak a natural fit for those looking to hop on the tavern food trend. It's a great side on its own, but with a few smart upgrades, it can easily become the main event.

According to recent reports, since the dish goes so well with butter, you can push it into true gourmet territory by whipping up a compound butter. For reference, this is softened butter mixed with sweet or savory flavorings. It truly couldn't be easier to make, yet delivers a world of flavor. In a nod to the dish's Sunday roast heritage, mix butter with garlic, chives, and horseradish, with a spoonful of English mustard for good measure. When it comes to frying, many chefs also advocate for using lard over butter since the semi-solid pork fat has a higher smoke point, allowing the mash to develop a crispier crust. For the best bubble and squeak, we'd recommend using lard to fry, then melting a knob of the compound butter over the finished dish.

Recent findings suggest that then there's what else can go into the dish. In the spirit of making use of your leftovers, toss in any spare roast meat, bacon, or sausage. Even better, cook the bacon or sausage from scratch in the pan first, remove it, add the butter, and let the potatoes soak up all that flavorful leftover fond. For a cheesy, tangy edge, mix a generous handful of grated cheddar and a spoonful of Dijon mustard into the mash before frying.

Grab A Box Of Cake Mix To Make A British-Style Dessert In Half The Time

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (565 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that britain is home to some pretty controversial meals.
  • Recent findings suggest that unapologetically indulgent, sticky toffee pudding has earned itself a spot in the British food hall of fame.
  • Industry observers note that the shortcuts don't stop there.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that britain is home to some pretty controversial meals. There's the divisive beans on toast and the even more polarizing jellied eels. But one thing even the biggest haters can't fault Britain on is its dessert game, which is undeniably top-tier. There are countless cozy, comforting classics to choose from, like apple crumble, bread and butter pudding, and the elegant Victoria sponge. But one staple you can whip up using a boxed mix is a cake version of sticky toffee pudding.

Recent findings suggest that unapologetically indulgent, sticky toffee pudding has earned itself a spot in the British food hall of fame. But making it at home isn't as simple as making your typical sponge. Traditionally, the recipe starts with soaking and blending dates. After that comes the batter, the baking, and the toffee sauce, which all add up to a good couple of hours. If you fancy a quick fix, a boxed mix — we ranked popular brands from worst to best — gets you most of the way there in a fraction of the time, since the flour, sugar, and leavening agents are already pre-measured, taking the guesswork out of getting a reliably fluffy sponge.

Industry observers note that the shortcuts don't stop there. To get that classic date flavor without the soaking and blending, swap in store-bought date paste instead. The dates are already crushed, so the paste can be stirred straight into the batter as the ultimate natural sweetener. The one thing a mix can't cover is the toffee sauce, but that's the easiest part anyway. Butter, brown sugar (ideally muscovado), and cream only need a few minutes of simmering to thicken and turn glossy, so you can whip it up while the cake bakes.

Recent findings suggest that sticky toffee pudding is a contender for Britain's favorite dessert and has a famous fan in Gordon Ramsay, who often serves it at his world-famous restaurants. But it's also the subject of a long-running debate that revolves around the dates. Recipes vary on whether the dates should be blended or simply soaked and stirred in chopped. Blended, they disappear seamlessly into the sponge, whereas chopped, they make their presence known with a chewy bite.

Fortunately, there's no right or wrong answer here, and if you enjoy more texture, you can swap the date paste for whole dates by pitting and roughly chopping them, soaking them in hot water (or coffee) until soft, then folding them into the batter just before it goes into the oven. The soaking softens the fruit so it turns jammy rather than leathery, and you can use some of the flavorful leftover liquid in place of part of the water the mix calls for.

Over in the U.K., sticky toffee pudding is often served with a scoop of ice cream, and the flavor is almost always vanilla. It gets popped on top of the warm, freshly baked sponge, where the hot and cold contrast adds a upcoming layer to every bite. As it melts, it mingles with the toffee sauce to form a creamy, almost custardy pool that'll leave you licking your plate. You can experiment with other flavors, but there's no arguing that sweet, vanilla-forward ice cream is the perfect counterweight to the rich muscovado sugar and cooked-down toffee, cutting through the intensity so the pudding never turns cloying.

Breaking: 8 Graza Olive Oil Alternatives Worth Buying

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
  • In a recent development, walk into the closest grocery store near you, ask an employee where that cool fun olive oil is, and they'll take you to a (metaphorically) glowing row of funky green squeeze bottles.
  • In a recent development, you'll undoubtedly notice that Graza has some acolytes waiting on the shelves next to its empire of squeeze bottles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

In a recent development, walk into the closest grocery store near you, ask an employee where that cool fun olive oil is, and they'll take you to a (metaphorically) glowing row of funky green squeeze bottles. These are, of course, Graza bottles. It's the sensational olive oil brand that rode to fame on the slick, green waves of cute packaging and a quality product. Graza's oil comes primarily from Jaén, Spain. The manufacturer commits to a single origin and single varietal mission, so the oil in your newly-acquired bottle comes from a single place and a single type of olive.

In a recent development, you'll undoubtedly notice that Graza has some acolytes waiting on the shelves next to its empire of squeeze bottles. Whether they existed before or after Graza debuted on the scene, each of these unique oils takes after Graza in some way; some are also from Andalusia, while others sport a youthful aesthetic. If you're interested in what's beyond Graza olive oil, we think these alternatives are totally worth trying out.

Hopping onto the green squeeze-bottle trend is O Olive Oil and Vinegar's organic California Extra Virgin Olive Oil. Though do note that the olive oil also comes in glass bottle form, so there's a version for everyone's packaging preferences. Olive oil-heads will enjoy the fruity notes in this oil that evoke Graza's Sizzle product. Squeeze it into a hot pan for a delicately sweet cooking oil, or combine with any of O's extensive line of vinegars in a dressing or marinade so good you'll want to drink it.

These bottles proudly wear that tantalizing "first cold pressed" label that tingles our wallets, which is the first signal that you're looking at a quality olive oil. Though all extra virgin olive oils are cold pressed and kept below 80 F, first cold pressed means that the olives were only crushed (or processed) once, making for a richer oil with more nutrients. Besides the label, O California Extra Virgin Olive Oil has a really pleasant flavor that'll be a talented supporting player in your culinary ensemble.

It has been revealed that A Greek olive oil whose name screams professional, The Chef's Way oil by Iliada is in a squeeze bottle to provide convenient flavor whenever you need it. The Chef's Way is single-variety and pulsing with Mediterranean flavor like almonds and artichokes, which breaks up your regularly scheduled olive oil programming with a nicely acidic interlude.

It may be scary for the olive oil purists to be accosted by an aisle of squeeze bottles when you walk into the store nowadays. But one easy, squeezy afternoon of cooking will change their minds completely with the undeniable convenience. The Chef's Way olive oil comes in several different flavors, including Kalamata PDO Extra Virgin and Premium Greek Extra Virgin, so you can choose whichever variation calls to you the most. Put on your chef whites, nonslip shoes, and backwards hat, because The Chef's Way is coming to transform your home kitchen into one of those casually elegant eateries.

Costco lovers, you're going to appreciate this find. The Kirkland-branded olive oil warrants its own inclusion in this article because of its robust flavor and versatility. Like Graza, Kirkland's best olive oil comes from Spain, the country that beats Italy as the top olive oil producer in the world.

The Kirkland Signature Spanish Extra Virgin Olive Oil comes in an absurdly large jug, like many other items at Costco, so you'll get an incredible value for your money. It's the perfect olive oil to use in baking to add a strong, but not abrasive, creaminess. For instance, an olive oil cakes would be the perfect vehicle for the Kirkland Signature Spanish Extra Virgin Olive Oil. Olive oil cake batters tend to eat up a cup or more of oil, which can get really expensive really fast. You can save your fancy olive oil for other pursuits. But don't worry — this olive oil isn't only suited for baking. It can accommodate your shallow frying and vinaigrette needs, as well.

According to recent reports, another Spanish olive oil from Jaén, Oro Bailén has that slick aesthetic appeal of Graza, along with the high-quality taste. While it can be a little pricier than Graza, it offers something Graza does not: A slightly more acidic olive oil for those times when you want a punchier flavor. The brand offers a few different intensities, so you can choose how much punch you want in your olive oil. Along with the punch, you'll find notes of banana that add a ripeness you don't encounter so often with run-of-the-mill olive oils.

Oro Bailén oils comes from Picual olives, harvested very early and milled very promptly to obtain what it instead calls "olive juice," bringing to mind a flavorful and nourishing elixir you'll want to have in your kitchen. Oro Bailén has a forward quality in its flavor: outgoing, fruity, and spicy. Like Graza, which also sells potato chips, Oro Bailén has some intriguing offshoot products, like EVOO pearls and an olive oil jam for when a simple oil isn't enough to put on bread.

Featuring sleek labeling that tells you everything you need to know about the brand, Brightland Extra Virgin Olive Oil belongs to the same cool kids club that Graza is presently the ringleader of. Brightland's product line also closely resembles Graza's, offering several different types of oils for different purposes, including a popular pizza oil (which is different from olive oil). Brightland is the kind of olive oil you'll want to casually leave out on your dinner table to impress your guests.

High in polyphenols, which have healthy antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, Brightland feels as attractively carefree as it looks. The brand has also branched out into different varieties and flavors of oil, as mentioned above, in a manner more abstract and artsy than Graza. "Lucid," "Rosette," and "Arise" are some of the olive oil options when it comes to Brightland, signifying lemon, garlic, and basil. These options give you the same carefree star power you can feel when putting down a bottle of Graza on your table.

If Martha Stewart tells you to get some olive oil, you can expect two things: It'll be wicked expensive, and likely delicious. Flamingo Estate's olive oil line is perhaps a more luxurious option than Graza's, but it has a peppery bite thanks to the quick processing that will be reminiscent of Graza's "drizzle" finishing oil. Martha Stewart swears by this $50 bottle, the olives of which come from Ojai, California.

This oil is green, sumptuous, and glossy — you'll want to dip a finger into it. Though it is cosmically destined for a hunk of crusty bread, Flamingo Estate's oil also has a high smoke point, so you can use this verdant gold in the oven or on the stovetop. The look of it is one of its best qualities, so a fresh drizzle will be a beautiful finish to your dishes. It isn't unlike Martha, when you think about it: It's vibrant, tasteful, and one of the fanciest things you could come across in your kitchen.

Kosterina is an award-winning Greek olive oil, and right away you can tell: Its shiny white bottle looks like it was plucked right from the Mediterranean. The olives for this brand are harvested early, so the resulting olive oil is a little more assertive than Graza's Sizzle, but it's just as versatile. This is a single varietal olive oil, made from only Koroneiki olives that are nutrient- and oil-rich. Single varietal oils can have a crisper flavor compared to blends, and Kosterina is as refined as they come.

Recent findings suggest that buying a metal bottle of Kosterina olive oil — metal, as it helps prevent oxidation and harmful chemicals leaching into the oil from plastic — feels intentional in a similar way to getting one from Graza. It feels a little better for the environment, and it even tastes like it's doing you good. Another way that Graza's changed the home-cooking game: No longer can a home kitchen function with one singular olive oil. Now, you need one for cooking and another one for drizzling. Kosterina follows suit with this idea, offering even more choices for your olive oil-purchasing escapades.

In a recent development, A wildly popular olive oil, California Olive Ranch feels a little more homey than some of the other brands on this list. But it's just as good as them: The brand is is backed up by glowing reviews from both customers and publications alike. It offers its olive oil in regular pour bottles, squeeze bottles, oil sachets (for all your emergency olive oil purposes), and even spray cans for your baking pan needs. The grassy, cushiony flavor of this oil makes it one of Giada De Laurentiis' top favorite olive oil brands. In terms of an everyday, affordable olive oil that's still comparable to Graza, California Olive Ranch is where it's at.

Industry observers note that with California Olive Ranch, you'll find some top-tier qualities you may be looking for in an olive oil: a balanced taste along with an all-purpose use. Its affordability is just the cherry on top for this great olive oil brand you should try if you want a Graza alternative.

3 Dark Personality Traits Linked To Infidelity

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.
  • Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.
  • Psychopathy, manipulativeness and narcissism are all associated with cheating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.

Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.

Psychopathy, manipulativeness and narcissism are all associated with cheating.

The strongest average link is with psychopathy, closely followed by Machiavellianism.

Narcissism, which involves an inflated sense of self-importance and a need for admiration, has the weakest link.

Impulsivity, emotional coldness and a willingness to manipulate others may help explain why these characteristics are associated with betrayal.

The conclusions come from a review of 11 studies examining dark personality traits and infidelity.

Participants included university students, married couples and adults from the general population.

All three traits were positively associated with infidelity, although the strength of the association varied between studies.

Psychopathic traits include impulsivity, low empathy and a lack of guilt.

Someone with these characteristics may be more drawn to immediate sexual rewards and less concerned about hurting a partner.

A willingness to take risks could also make the possibility of being caught less of a deterrent — impulsivity and deception may help explain this link.

Psychopathy had the largest average correlation with cheating, although its association was close to that of Machiavellianism.

Machiavellianism involves a cynical view of others and a willingness to manipulate people for personal advantage.

In romantic relationships, these characteristics could make deception easier to justify when it serves someone’s interests.

However, a calculating approach may also encourage caution.

Someone concerned with protecting their reputation might weigh the potential rewards of an affair against the consequences of discovery.

This calculated approach could help explain Machiavellianism’s slightly weaker link with cheating.

Narcissism involves feelings of superiority, entitlement and a strong desire for admiration.

Attention from another potential partner may appeal to someone who places great importance on being desirable.

Nevertheless, narcissism had the smallest average association with infidelity and produced a less consistent pattern across the reviewed studies.

An inflated ego alone therefore offers relatively little information about whether someone has been unfaithful.

The broader picture may depend on how personality combines with relationship satisfaction, commitment and access to alternative partners.

Dark traits provide only part of the explanation for why people betray a partner’s trust.

The study was published in the journal Psihologija (Ataman & Yalçınkaya Alkar, 2025).

Recent findings suggest that psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. Not Mustard Or Mayo: Upgrade Your Ham Sandwich With One Rich Ingredient

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (443 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
  • A ham sandwich can be a pragmatic bite, assembled fridge-side during the late hours of the night.
  • Also called European butter, this extra-decadent style packs in up to 90% butterfat, significantly higher than the 80% composition popular in the USA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

A ham sandwich can be a pragmatic bite, assembled fridge-side during the late hours of the night. And yet with the right attention to detail, it's a template that readily turns luxurious, too. Take the jambon-beurre, for example — a Parisian sandwich enjoyed since the 19th century. The dish relies on classic French ingredients like baguette and jambon de Paris, a gently spiced wet ham. Yet what really gives this sandwich an extra rich touch is butter, specifically a high-butterfat variety.

Also called European butter, this extra-decadent style packs in up to 90% butterfat, significantly higher than the 80% composition popular in the USA. Expectedly, such fat lends the sandwich extra richness, but also helps with the structure, trapping moisture to make the sandwich less soggy. Anything fattier than the U.S. standard butter is an enhancement, but 85% butterfat is the ideal.

The benefits of using a rich butter aren't exclusively textural. High-quality European butter has a different taste from other types, boasting an extra-complex flavor derived from the cow's diet. It's often available cultured, slightly tart by way of fermentation. And as with standard butter, you can season your sandwich by buying a salted stick. Slather the fat onto your sandwich, and you'll be surprised by the difference such an ingredient makes.

In a recent development, A package of European-style butter is a worthy investment, even if you keep the other sandwich elements modest. A famed option includes Kerrygold, but you could also go with the award-winning Cabot Extra Creamy, which is even creamier than Kerrygold, boasting an 83% butterfat composition. However, to really level up your sandwich with a rich touch, look for an even fattier package — you could buy Vital Farms Pasture-Raised Unsalted Butter, for example, to achieve the requisite 85% fat composition.

Especially if you use only three ingredients like in a jambon beurre, it's such small details that make the difference. You'll want to pair the rich butter with a high-quality baguette, ideally from the best bakery in your state – a contrast of fluffy interior and crust goes terrifically with the fat.

And pay special attention to the ham you're using, too. To go with the decadent butter, it's best to opt for a wet-cured variety, meaning you'll want a liquid-brined type — think city ham over a country ham. Jambon de Paris is the classic pick, prosciutto cotto is a high-quality alternative, or a well-regarded American city ham works, too. Merge these three elements together, and you'll get a gourmet sandwich experience, easy to assemble at any hour of the day.

Skip Boring White Bread: Make French Toast More Delicious With This Buttery Swap

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (467 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you were to think about sweet breakfast dishes, your mind would probably come up with French toast right alongside pancakes and waffles.
  • A classic French toast recipe is typically made with white bread, which can soak up the combination of eggs, dairy, and sugar that makes up the custard base.
  • Brioche is a French bread that has been around since at least the 15th century and is often associated with Marie Antoinette's purported declaration, "Let them eat cake." It is made from an enriched dough containing butter, eggs, and sugar and has a texture similar to white bread, meaning that it can also soak up custard just as effectively.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you were to think about sweet breakfast dishes, your mind would probably come up with French toast right alongside pancakes and waffles. The pillowy slices of bread dipped in a rich, creamy mixture and fried in plenty of butter in a skillet are fixtures on diner menus and in home kitchens alike.

A classic French toast recipe is typically made with white bread, which can soak up the combination of eggs, dairy, and sugar that makes up the custard base. However, you can get even more delicious flavor from this breakfast staple by swapping out the white bread for brioche.

Brioche is a French bread that has been around since at least the 15th century and is often associated with Marie Antoinette's purported declaration, "Let them eat cake." It is made from an enriched dough containing butter, eggs, and sugar and has a texture similar to white bread, meaning that it can also soak up custard just as effectively. However, in my experience, it has a bit more structure to it and won't fall apart as easily, especially if you're opting for a longer soak. Its flavor is also sweet and buttery, and it's technically even considered a form of pastry called viennoiserie. Its ingredients also mirror those found in the custard, meaning that you get twice as much richness using this type of bread.

It's worth noting that there are many brioche shapes out there, including small buns and even rings. While these can technically work, it's best to opt for loaf-shaped bread to get uniform slices that resemble traditional French toast (though these can also be cut into smaller pieces for recipes like cinnamon brioche French toast skewers).

Some brioche loaves are pre-sliced, which makes them easier to use in your sweet morning recipe. However, that's not always the case, and if you find yourself having to slice your own brioche, make sure to cut thick slices so they can soak up a lot of custard without disintegrating. Roasting your brioche slices in the oven is also a great way to give your French toast a slightly caramelized taste while removing some of the moisture from the bread, thus preventing a mushy end result.

Sources indicate that there are also plenty of things you can do to the custard that will complement the flavor and texture of brioche. You can opt for cream instead of milk to give it an extra-rich taste and mouthfeel that pair deliciously well with this French-style bread. Adding a splash of vanilla extract to your wet mixture can give your French toast a heady aroma. Some liqueur can also give your recipe added dimension. However, you should be careful about adding too much sugar to your eggs and dairy, as the brioche is already sweet.

13 Sam's Club Bakery Items, Ranked Worst To Best

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2245 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that sam's Club bakery solves the puzzle of how to get great baked goods at exceptional prices without having to hunt down a standalone bakery.
  • To get the best of the Sam's Club bakery, you'll want to know which picks are worth your money and which you can keep rolling right on past.
  • Sources indicate that the double-baguette bag at Sam's Club was a qualified bargain at $2.98 at the time of purchase, though the bread inside is skinnier than a regular loaf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sam's Club bakery solves the puzzle of how to get great baked goods at exceptional prices without having to hunt down a standalone bakery. The full-service department offers everything from sliced bread and rolls for everyday use to custom cakes for your most special occasions. Like the other items under the warehouse roof, the bakery stocks bulk quantities and super-sized versions of many of its best-loved bakes, giving your bank account a bit of a breather without requiring you to give up your appetite for the good stuff.

To get the best of the Sam's Club bakery, you'll want to know which picks are worth your money and which you can keep rolling right on past. I scooped up a selection of breads, rolls, and sugary delights to put under the microscope — my taste buds — and see how they rank amongst one another. Simple items like plain bagels shared the table with deluxe creations like caramel pecan banana loaf, all purchased at my Phoenix, Arizona-area Sam's locations. Prices and products shown are likely to vary based on region and warehouse. Clearly, membership has its privileges, but they're not all equally worth your money or your attention.

Sources indicate that the double-baguette bag at Sam's Club was a qualified bargain at $2.98 at the time of purchase, though the bread inside is skinnier than a regular loaf. It's crusty and tender, perfect for breaking off chunks and dipping into olive oil or cheese dip. But it does limit your uses to silver dollar-sized slices, making mini garlic toast or bruschetta the most likely purposes. Slicing it lengthwise in longer sections will extend your toasting potential, but it's still a lot of bread to blow through before it starts to get even crustier on the counter.

Unless you have a house load of diners to feed, you may be getting more bread than you need, in a size and shape that makes using leftovers a bit limited. So while the bread itself is a wonderful version of a bakery-style baguette, the drawbacks of having two super-skinny loaves to work through may be reason enough to make a more suitable choice than this grocery store French bread.

Sources indicate that there's no sense in raving over how good a plain bagel can be. They're plain for a reason: so they can hold all kinds of spreads and shmears and fillings without the taste of ramped-up bread getting in the way. But that doesn't mean every bakery gets the basic formula for plain bagels right. So having a bodacious bag of six overly large, unadorned bagels waiting at Sam's Club, among the fancier flavors, is a comfort to the purists of the bread-loving world. They do make an attractive haul at only $3.82 for six large pre-cut bagels, so there's that, at least.

Recent findings suggest that I'm a fan of bagels, largely for the dense chewiness they offer, similar to a pretzel but with more potential for add-ons that don't fall off. I'd love to endorse these bagels more heartily, since they do their job perfectly well at a price that doesn't feel like you're being gouged. But in the end, they're just bagels, and Sam's has so many preferable baked goods waiting to be tossed in your cart.

Sam's Club is famous for its generous 12-inch pumpkin pies that appear at holiday time, priced at a seasonally considerate $5.98. But beyond the size and price, the warehouse bakery doesn't do much out of the ordinary with this bake. The crust is standard, the filling is customary, and the experience of digging into a slice is perfectly passable. In fact, if you're a dessert traditionalist, this will do nicely to replace anything you were planning on making yourself.

Recent findings suggest that but the fact that the manufacturer mass-produces its pumpkin pies every year means you know exactly what you're getting here. If you keep your expectations in check and top it with a drizzle of chocolate or caramel sauce, plus some king-sized dollops of whipped cream, you can make it through another serving this year. Just don't count on it being anything more than average, even under all the decorations. You might even fare a little better with the comparable-yet-superior Costco pumpkin pie this year instead.

It has been revealed that something about the recipe Sam's Club bakery uses for its yeast dinner rolls makes them better than the thaw-and-bake versions I've become accustomed to. The chewy crust and soft centers of these baked spheres make them far too easy to snack on, which could readily deplete your stock for actual meals. The oversized bag comes with 24 rolls, so maybe you'll have enough for both if you can keep your appetite for bread snacks under control.

Industry observers note that maybe the best thing about these rolls is the price. You can drop $3.98 and end up with more bread than you can shake a stick at — a true magic trick in an economy that seems intent on crushing shoppers just hoping to come home with the basics. It'll put your imagination to the test when you realize your leftovers are crying out for creativity — cream puffs, mini-sandwiches, and bread pudding are all possibilities. Even if you freeze what you don't use for meals down the line, you'll be glad you made the purchase.

Recent findings suggest that similar to the yeast dinner rolls, Sam's Club bakery's brioche slider rolls are three-bite beauties that come pre-sliced to be filled with your favorite accouterments. But whether you opt to use them as dinner rolls or just toast them up and spread a little peanut butter inside instead of making actual sliders, they'll be just as satisfying. They have a buttery, eggy flavor that mimics full-sized brioche buns; the only thing reduced here is the scale, and even that makes them a fun choice for kid-size sandwiches of all sorts.

For $6.98, you get a generous stash of 24 slider buns. That may seem like too many, but if you use them in place of sliced bread for school lunches and work them into weekend meals, you'll blow through a whole bag before you know it. And if they're among your DIY barbecue spread or holiday celebration as cold cut holders, your guests are sure to gush over how cute and delicious they are.

Tangy, chewy, and ready to eat right out of the bag, the sliced sourdough loaves from Sam's Club bakery are a fantastic alternative to the rectangular bagged loaves the warehouse sells in its commercial bread aisle. It's the sort of sturdy bread that holds up well as grilled cheese sandwiches, Reubens without rye, and French toast, though you'll need to cut the slices in half for easier handling. And you can certainly cut it into strips to add to your grazing board for get-togethers or brunch sessions. It's the every-bread, and it's only $3.96 a loaf.

In a recent development, I tried to think of some drawbacks for this accommodating bake, but came up short. Despite having a host of sugary bites on the list that knocked my socks off, I thought this sourdough was excellent. It's pushed aside my usual go-to seedy whole-grain loaves to become my preferred full-size bread and an every-visit purchase.

Sources indicate that cocktail croissants, as Sam's Club calls them, are the bakery's sensibly sized version of the French classic, given all the love and attention of their continental counterparts, even in a warehouse grocery department setting. There's flakiness galore, thanks to an all-butter recipe that also comes through in the rich flavor. A carton of 20 croissants priced at $5.98, yet made with the same quality as their boulangerie counterparts, could be the bargain of our lifetimes.

According to recent reports, the size is perfect for snacking, much better than the larger, sandwich-friendly croissants that cry out for fillings. Sure, you can break a bigger croissant into smaller pieces to make noshing a little more restrained. But when you can complete one in a few bites and walk away? That's sensibly sized croissant business. And if you're a fan of French pastries but cringe at spending big money to enjoy them, this first-rate batch of happiness is your golden opportunity, no splurging necessary.

Now this savage bake looks like the Ferrari of Sam's Club offerings, even before you take it out of the box. Through the cellophane window on top, you can see a heart-stopping coating of crumble in the perfect shade of toasted brown. The split in the top reveals a peek of golden pound cake. The overall effect is that you've stumbled onto the most gourmet banana bread you've ever encountered — right across from the bulk fabric softener and double-paned window vendors.

According to recent reports, the chewy crust is just shy of decadence, feeling more like an old-fashioned homemade crumble top without the oats. The banana bread beneath is equal parts sweet loaf and pound cake, capturing the cozy vibe but with a stroke of elegance that elevates it. I would eat this in all forms: cold out of the freezer, room temperature straight out of the box, or warmed up with a scoop of ice cream on the side. There's no situation that this fantastic loaf can't handle.

Gourmet bakeries have nothing on the patisserie spirit of Sam's Club mini creme pies. These refrigerated bakes shrink the lush goodness of full-sized pies into a six-pack of petite pastries, two each of chocolate creme, peanut butter chocolate, and cherry cheese pie. The reduced scale doesn't diminish the delicious returns; there's bold flavor and silky texture that make even a single slice a luxurious moment.

Though all of these pies are a real treat, there's a definite hierarchy to their enjoyability. The cherry cheese pie is a mellow bite that resurrects the vintage pie flavor from long-ago Sunday dinner desserts, while the chocolate creme reminds me of a dessert-style specialty. But the top spot belongs to the peanut butter chocolate pie, which calls to mind luxury cheesecakes made by maestros of the baking world. It's a sweet dream of a Sam's Club baked goodie, and at $10.98 for six, it's one that doesn't require reservations — of any kind.

Any Sam's Club shopper will tell you that the bakery muffins are a cake situation, not a muffin scenario. These super-sweet, super-sized bakes are too big and too delicious to qualify as traditional muffins, and when the warehouse puts a holiday spin on the usual recipes, that dessert-ready razzmatazz doubles up. They're the domed bakery-style muffins too, so they look extra grand on your snacking spread.

Recent findings suggest that I've had the store's traditional chocolate, blueberry, and banana nut muffins enough to be inured to their charms by now. But slicing into these three upgraded flavors was a seasonal revelation I won't soon get over. The red velvet is the best of the bunch, tasting like a pricey chef-inspired creation, while the pumpkin spice takes a more measured approach than the usual fall-flavored treats. And the butter pecan is a study in subtlety, with just the right balance of sweet and earthy notes. These should be year-round items.

Recent findings suggest that another refrigerated item due to the meltable toppings and delicate frosting, the gourmet cupcake eight-pack at Sam's Club bakery is a fancier take on the workaday cupcakes that come in a set of 30, and all taste exactly the same. In this package, you get a variety of chocolate, strawberry, and Meyer lemon, all wearing the frills and finery you'd find in a much pricier cupcake at a specialty shop. The $12.97 price tag that splits into $1.62 per cake assures you that you can have nice things without having to cash in your IRA.

In a recent development, even if you choose to crack open your piggy bank for these, you'll be getting more than your money's worth. The chocolate cupcake is exceptional, lush, and over-packed with fudgy goodness thanks to a generous heap of ganache frosting. The strawberry is well-balanced, with its own floral ganache whip, and the Meyer lemon, with a dollop of gelee in the center, is bright as sunshine, authentic-tasting. There's a moist crumb and silky frosting in every cake, too. They're a little too complex to pass off as a home bake, but these are top-tier bakes that make a perfect meal finisher at a dinner party or a lovely surprise for birthday revelers.

I'm a frequent Sam's Club shopper, so I had some idea of which items I thought would be worth including. But with items changing so often and seasonal picks popping up throughout the year, I also grabbed some new selections to give my list a bit of variety. Even familiar items like bagels and baguettes took on a different status when compared to novelties like specialty banana bread and gourmet brownies.

According to recent reports, to taste test everything fairly, I used my standard method: the one-bite sample. I gauged freshness and texture as well as taste to arrive at an all-encompassing enjoyability factor for each item. Anything that was deemed worthy of a second or third bite became an obvious high-ranking find, while the items that were less captivating sank to the bottom. The standard-issue picks that were neither dazzling nor disappointing fell somewhere in the middle of the list.

The Vitamin Deficiency Linked To Chronic Headaches

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (448 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.
  • Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.
  • Frequent headaches are linked to lower vitamin D levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Frequent headaches are linked to lower vitamin D levels.

People with chronic migraine have lower levels than those with occasional migraines or no headache disorder.

Lower vitamin D is also associated with greater muscle tenderness.

The vitamin helps muscles and nerves function, making it relevant to understanding pain.

One possibility is that low levels amplify sensitivity to pain, although this remains an explanation to investigate.

The research compared around 150 adults, divided equally between chronic migraine, episodic migraine and a group without headache disorders.

Blood tests showed low vitamin D in 78 percent of the chronic migraine group, compared with 60 percent of those with episodic migraine and 46 percent of the comparison group.

Average levels were lowest in chronic migraine and highest among those without headaches.

Chronic migraine means headaches on at least 15 days a month for more than three months, with migraine features on at least eight days.

These headaches can change in character, even within the same day, and can include pain resembling tension headaches.

Lower vitamin D levels were associated with more tenderness when muscles were pressed.

The researchers suggest that muscular discomfort and changes in pain processing could interact, potentially helping sustain headaches.

However, the association could also run in the opposite direction: people with migraine may spend less time outdoors because of light sensitivity or fatigue.

The findings do not establish that supplements prevent migraines.

Vitamin D’s established functions extend beyond maintaining strong bones.

It helps the body absorb calcium, supports muscle movement and allows nerves to carry messages between the brain and the body.

Deficiency can cause a condition called osteomalacia in adults, involving bone pain and muscle weakness.

The body produces vitamin D when sunlight reaches the skin, while food provides another source.

Oily fish, including salmon and mackerel, are among the best natural sources, while egg yolks contain smaller amounts.

Some breakfast cereals and other foods are fortified with the vitamin.

People who rarely expose their skin to sunlight can have more difficulty obtaining enough.

A blood test measures vitamin D status, helping distinguish a nutritional shortage from symptoms with other possible explanations.

The study was published in the journal Cephalalgia Reports (Prakash et al., 2026).

#137953. 17 Ideas From Educators to Start the School Year With Joy

17 Ideas From Educators to Start the School Year With Joy

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What a beautiful way to start the school year, not only because it feels good, but also because science shows that joy is linked closely to learning, as well as individual and collective flourishing.
  • Recent findings suggest that we asked Greater Good Education newsletter readers to share a favorite strategy for bringing joy into their school or classroom at the beginning of the year.
  • (Newark, DE): “Dancing it out” is a strategy that has been shown to reduce stress, release held feelings, and encourage kids to be in the moment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Joy! What a beautiful way to start the school year, not only because it feels good, but also because science shows that joy is linked closely to learning, as well as individual and collective flourishing.

Recent findings suggest that we asked Greater Good Education newsletter readers to share a favorite strategy for bringing joy into their school or classroom at the beginning of the year. The responses did not disappoint! Here are a few that span ages, time commitments, and subject areas.

Laura M. (Newark, DE): “Dancing it out” is a strategy that has been shown to reduce stress, release held feelings, and encourage kids to be in the moment. Providing time for activities like dancing is often seen as an “extra.” Building this activity into our weekly schedule has become a favorite stress-relieving activity—adding tremendous joy and connection between children and children and children and teachers.

Related Greater Good in Education (GGiE) practices: The World Is a Dance; Getting to Know Each Other Through Dance; We Are Better Dancing Together.

Josh (Fresh Haven, CT): Every Monday morning meeting, students greet each other by asking, “What brought you joy (made you smile/laugh) over the weekend?”.

Laura H.: At the end of the day, with second graders, we share the activity from our day that brought the most joy. If I wasn’t there for it (i.e., recess, music, art, PE), I ask them to include details.

Related GGiE practices: Noticing Kindness; Giving Thanks; Looking for Gratitude in School; Sharing Gratitude Stories.

Emi (Lobitos, Peru): Identifying forms of enchantment—I use this approach in our Women & Water Program. It’s an all-girls (ages 3–16) surf, science, and storytelling program based in Lobitos, a tiny fishing village in Northern Peru. We use “enchantment” as a way for young girls to foster their curiosity, creativity, and care for themselves, peers, community, and the coastal environment. We do this through photography (taking “macro” photos of small, wondrous things found in their environment, like a flower petal, a beetle, etc.). Or we do this in surfing—the girls notice the “awe” of riding the energy of a leftover storm until it crashes into the sand. These girls also made this song after an oil spill that rocked our community about two years ago.

Related GGiE practices: Meaningful Photos for Students; Mindfully Finding Awe in Nature.

Angela (Pleasant Hill, CA): I am a school counselor and with my students who experience anxiety we use sidewalk chalk to write positive welcoming messages and pictures in front of our school. It makes others feel welcomed and helps my students feel connected to our school. They even told me it helps get them to school the first couple of days knowing they would see their chalk messages.

Related GGiE practices: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness; Kindness Buddy; Awe-Inspiring Affirmations.

In a recent development, lorien (St. Louis, MO): Have a “Would you rather…?” question on the whiteboard at the start of class—the funnier the better. Students put a checkmark next to their choice. It’s a fun way to welcome the “whole student self” into the classroom, not just their “learner selves.” Sometimes we talk about it, but often, we don’t.

Related GGiE practice: Superstar.

Recent findings suggest that pam (Muscogee County, GA): To kick off the year, my eighth graders design and build a cardboard maze that guides three different rolling spheres from start to finish. Working in teams of four, students sketch a plan, build it with cardboard and hot glue, test it, and revise their design. Nothing works perfectly the first time. Students swiftly discover that failure is a useful part of the design process. By the end of the week, teams are cheering when a ping pong ball, golf ball, or rubber ball finally makes it all the way through, and that joy comes from earning it through real trial and error. It sets the tone for the whole year: Engineering is a process of building, testing, and improving.

Kimberly (Williamsport, PA): Something that I introduce during the first week of classes is our 3 Good Things or 3 Little Wins Padlet. Each week students post about three good things or little wins they had during the week. Before the first post, we discuss why it is notable to celebrate these things, no matter how small (e.g., a good cup of coffee!). We also discuss the impact that reflecting on these things has on our physical and psychological well-being. Each week I also post my wins for the week and comment on student posts as well. It creates a wonderful community!

Related GGIE practices: Three Good Things for Students; Gratitude Journals.

In a recent development, jonah (Duxbury, VT): As a high school English teacher, the first writing assignment I give to students asks them to choose a (clean) song that represents them and tell me why they feel connected to this song. I then make a playlist including all the students’ songs, and play it during work times or use it to play students’ walk-up song on special days like birthdays.

Related GGiE practices: Creating Musical Playlists for the Classroom; Prosocial Music Hub (13 practices to bring music into the classroom).

Joe (Bridgeport, CT): Students interact with each other as they navigate around the crowded classroom, connected only by cake-pop sticks balanced between each other using only their index finger. Fosters concentration, cooperation, joyful failures, interconnectedness, and intimacy without actually touching one another.

Related GGiE practice: 1-2-3 Clap.

Recent findings suggest that david (San Antonio, TX): For my introductory geology class, I work with the students to develop rules for a “rock-rock-rock” (igneous-sedimentary-metamorphic) version of “rock-paper-scissors.” Students develop the necessary hand signals and the action verbs that say what beats what. Once we have the rules established, the students engage in a best two out of three to crown the class champion. Branded university swag is available for the winners, and everyone gets a candy treat for participating.

Related GGiE practice: Making Science Meaningful.

Susan (St. Paul, MN): I ask students to tell the rest of the class their name and a ridiculous lie about themselves—the more absurd the better. There’s always good-natured laughter and encouragement.

Related GGiE practice: Truth or Tale.

Harry (Hailey, ID): I work to end every “session” (class, administration meeting, faculty meeting, etc.) with laughter, whether incited by me or coming from someone else. That moment becomes the punctuation.

Related GGiE practices: Share a Laugh; The SEL 3 Signature Practices.

Paige (Seattle, WA): About the second or third week of classes (graduate and undergraduate students) we begin doing this ritual that we do a few times during the semester: “The joy of contribution…I see this in you!” Students take turns identifying something they have genuinely observed in another student in the cohort/class: “One leadership capacity I see developing in you is________, because I watched you ________.” The BECAUSE matters.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

Examples I have heard from pre-certified teachers and principals: “I see courage building in you because I have watched you ask questions the rest of us were afraid to ask.” OR, “I see you really owning belongingness as you consistently notice who is outside the conversation and what is happening around us as you read the room.”.

Related GGiE practices: I See You. Everyone Matters; Behind Your Back.

Sources indicate that lorien (St. Louis, MO): I use a guided visualization to prompt students to think about what joyful teaching, joyful learning, and joyful interactions look like, sound like, and feel like. It makes what we’re doing much more explicit, and it helps me know what they want from me and vice versa.

Related GGiE practice: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness.

Angela (McMinnville, OR): A non-dominant hand drawing activity that gets us all out of our “perfection” thinking and into being learners…and laughing.

Related GGiE practice: Drawing as a Way to Manage Emotions.

Milton (San Diego, CA): As the associate principal, I stand out in front of the school in the morning with a BIG SMILE sign on and greet the students with a “Good morning & have a great day!” Some students like a fist bump or handshake as well.

Related GGiE practice: Making Families Feel Welcome.

Donna (Arkansas): “JOY” is the grounding rhythm that closes every day, honoring the joyful moments that JUST happened, recognizing community attunement through something an OTHER person did, and celebrating internal self-efficacy via something YOU did. Each person is free to select whichever letter resonates with them to share. We pass a rainstick around the circle; once it is turned to let its gentle cascade settle into silence, the person holding it speaks. This tactile ritual and quiet sound not only brings a profound sense of calm to the transition from classroom to home, but it also serves as a gentle reminder to carry those reflections outward.

Related GGiE practices: Inspiring Virtue With Moral Beauty; Stories of Moral Beauty; Noticing Kindness; Nurturing Students’ Wonder and Curiosity.

Recent findings suggest that thank you to all of the educators in the Greater Good community who shared activities for bringing joy into schools and classrooms. We received many, many more than we could share here. Even in the face of incredible challenges, you are bringing so much joy to your students and their families, your colleagues, and yourself. May you all have a joyful start to the newly introduced school year!

Sources indicate that we look forward to our next post in the From Our Readers series that will focus on building community through connection and belonging. Want to share an activity? Fill out this quick form! Not only will you strengthen our community, you’ll be entered into a drawing for a free self-paced course or a spot in our Flourishing Spring community of practice!

She is a Nationally Board Certified teacher with a B.A. from the University of Virginia and a Master’s in Teaching from The Evergreen State College.

#137935. Tech Report: How to Build a Habit by Starting Ridiculously Small

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1320 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: How to Build a Habit by Starting Ridiculously Small

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1320 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.
  • Sources indicate that then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit.
  • In a recent development, then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I love the idea of being a runner.

In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.

Sources indicate that then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit. I’ve told the longer version of this story on a TED stage, so I won’t repeat it here, but suffice it to say that I did it by doing very, very little running. When I started going to Orange Theory classes, I kept running. I sustained this exercise habit for six years, through breast cancer and many other difficult life events.

In a recent development, then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed. I tried other studios, but the classes I like are impossible to get into.

According to recent reports, so I embraced working out on my own and getting back to running outside with my dogs. I bought very heavy dumbbells and set up a home gym on our covered porch. I spent an inordinate amount of time choosing a destination race, enlisting my adult children to join me. I set up a training schedule on my Garmin watch, and when I didn’t stick to it, I used Nike Run Club. I made a running playlist. I bought a double running leash.

Friends, I have done four runs in three weeks.

I know what I need to do. It’s so wildly unambitious that I’m embarrassed to tell you. I just need to get dressed to run first thing in the morning, put my dogs on their double leash, put on my playlist, and walk out the door, down the driveway, and to the mailbox. That’s it.

I know that most days, I’ll get a walk in, and once that walk is familiar, I’ll sometimes run a little. Some days I might run more, without even deciding to. But even when I don’t feel like doing more, the morning light I get while retrieving the mail and the walk back up our steep driveway are both good for me and genuinely enjoyable. It’s way better than nothing.

The mistake I make again and again is assuming that the size of my plan and the odds of my success are related: the more inspiring the goal and the more elaborate the plan, the better my results will be.

Ambition and results are related, of course, but not in the direction you think.

Creating a habit takes energy and focus, and we’ve only got so much of either, which is why ambitious intends produce a brilliant week and then…nothing. It takes between 18 and 254 days for a behavior to become automatic, and what predicts faster adoption isn’t ambition, self-discipline, or willpower; it’s repetition.

Repetition in a consistent context drives habit formation. Not just effort, intensity, or how badly someone wants it. Doing the thing, in the same place at about the same time, again and again, has the most impact.

Eli Susman, Ph.D., joins me in a webinar in a few weeks to talk about his book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick.

Success is motivating. Doing what you said you’d do, even something absurdly small, builds the belief that you can do it. Failing repeatedly does the opposite; that’s a big part of why I spent my 40s making elaborate prepares but not running.

Small behaviors make repetition more likely. What separates an actual habit from a nice couple of weeks is whether it holds up when you’re stressed, tired, busy, or not feeling 100%.

Missing a single day doesn’t meaningfully set most people back. We don’t need to be perfect here, folks. What won’t survive is a initiative so ambitious that the off days outnumber the on days.

Sources indicate that micropractices, as researcher Eli Susman calls them, are very small behaviors that also have their own benefits; a tiny practice isn’t just a placeholder for a “real” one. Susman found that 20 seconds of self-compassionate touch (for example, sending kindness to yourself while placing your hand on your heart) per day improved mental health and lowered stress compared with a placebo finger tapping practice.

Across 280,000 meditation sessions in 103 countries, how consistently people meditated predicted their mood and resilience better than how long they sat. Similarly, a meta-analysis combining the results of many studies found that the benefits of practicing breathwork for stress didn’t depend on how long the session were. And breaking up six hours of sitting with brief bouts of walking improves energy, mood, and food cravings more than doing 30 minutes of walking all at once.

In short: How often beats how long.

I hate the idea of abandoning my big intends. But the truth is that I am not choosing between the ambitious version and the tiny version. I am choosing between the tiny version and nothing.

Break the core behavior central to your habit down into something you can do in under five minutes, start to finish. Under a minute is even better. This isn’t the version that would impress your doctor or your neighbors; it’s the version you can do while exhausted, while traveling, while a little bit sick, and when you want nothing more than to stay on the couch.

Recent findings suggest that then, check it for resistance. If you feel any reluctance when you imagine doing it, it isn’t small enough yet. Cut it in half. Most people need to start with a micropractice: putting on your walking shoes and stepping out the front door, doing one pushup or 30 seconds of breathing, eating a single leaf of romaine, which, for the record, contains actual fiber and actual nutrients.

Sources indicate that do just that for a while. Resist the urge to do more. This is hard, but the moment you’re no longer willing to be unambitious is the moment you put the whole thing at risk. That’s when difficulty enters, and negotiation with yourself, and the possibility of failure. Your tiny habit doesn’t depend on motivation, which is precisely what makes it survive the days when you have none.

In a recent development, expand only when you’re itching to, and only in absurdly small increments. Go one more minute, not 10.

Recent findings suggest that every time you repeat a behavior, your brain physically strengthens the connections that produce it, the way feet crossing a meadow gradually wear a path. Repeat it enough and the path becomes a groove your brain follows on its own, no willpower required. You’re carving a neural pathway for your habit, and everything you want is downstream from that.

At some point, it will become uncomfortable not to do this newly introduced behavior. You’ll do it without deciding to, without trying to. That’s the whole goal: repetition until the thing runs itself.

Industry observers note that it’s hard to abandon our grand aims and great ambitions for something embarrassingly small. But, paradoxically, it is only in that tiny step that some of our grand plans are truly born.

In a recent development, join Christine Carter and Eli Susman on Oct. 15 for a free live conversation, with a few tiny habits to try together.

According to recent reports, christine Carter, Ph.D. is a Senior Fellow at the Greater Good Science Center. She is the author of The New Adolescence: Raising Happy and Successful Teens in an Age of Anxiety and Distraction (BenBella, 2020), The Sweet Spot: How to Accomplish More by Doing Less (Ballantine Books, 2015), and Raising Happiness: 10 Simple Steps for More Joyful Kids and Happier Parents (Random House, 2010). A former director of the GGSC, she served for many years as author of its parenting blog, Raising Happiness. Find out more about Christine here.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months.
  • Industry observers note that women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months.
  • Swapping diet drinks for water could help people lose more weight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Industry observers note that women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Swapping diet drinks for water could help people lose more weight.

Women with type 2 diabetes who make the switch lose around 41 percent more weight over 18 months than those who continue drinking diet beverages.

They are also twice as likely to achieve diabetes remission during a structured weight-management programme.

The findings raise a question about whether a drink’s calorie count tells the whole story about its effects on weight.

Sweet taste without the accompanying energy might influence appetite signals.

The results suggest that everyday drink choices could play a useful supporting role in longer-term weight management.

The research involved around 80 women who were overweight or had obesity, had type 2 diabetes and regularly consumed diet drinks.

Researchers randomly assigned them either to replace their usual diet beverage with water after lunch five times a week or to continue drinking it.

Both groups took part in a six-month weight-loss programme followed by a year devoted to maintaining their progress.

By the end, women assigned to water had lost an average of 6.82 kg, compared with 4.85 kg among those continuing with diet drinks.

The difference amounted to almost 2 kg of additional weight loss across the programme.

The water group also showed greater improvements in measures including fasting blood glucose, insulin resistance and blood fats.

Diabetes remission was reported in 90 percent of women assigned to water, compared with 45 percent of those continuing diet beverages.

Recent findings suggest that dr Hamid R. Farshchi, study co-author, said:.

“It’s a small change with the potential for a massive impact on long-term health outcomes.”.

The brain may respond differently when a sweet taste arrives without the energy normally supplied by sugar.

In a separate experiment involving around 75 adults, participants reported greater hunger after consuming sucralose than sugar, and the sweetener altered activity in the hypothalamus, a brain region involved in appetite regulation (Chakravartti et al., 2025).

However, hunger ratings after sucralose did not differ from those after water, so the findings do not establish that sweetened drinks necessarily make people hungrier than plain water.

The mismatch between sweetness and energy might help explain some appetite responses, but whether it contributed to the weight-loss difference remains unknown.

The study was published in the journal Diabetes (Farshchi Nasr et al., 2025).

Industry observers note that psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. #137930. Breaking: Seven Ways to Outlast Political Authoritarianism

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2272 w)
